ⓐ.summary: The decline in violent crime in the United States is closely related to lead exposure.

c1.text: The decline in crime in the United States is closely related to lead exposure.

c2.text: In children, exposure to lead affects brain development and induces increased aggression and impulsivity, influencing future criminal potential.

c3.text: Rates of violent and property crime are highest in the late teens to early twenties.

c4.text: There is an approximate 20-year lag between childhood lead exposure and the manifestation of criminal behavior in young adulthood.

c5.text: Lead emissions from cars rose postwar until the 1970s, and lead was phased out of gasoline starting in the 1970s.

c6.text: The sharp decline in violent crime began in the early 1990s and continued through 2020.

h1.text: Average blood lead levels of American children aged 1–5 in 2000 dropped to half the level of 1990.

h2.text: Decreased lead exposure in children around 1990–2000 corresponds to continued reduction in crime among young adults up to 2020.

a.note: A drop in blood lead levels in 2000 accounts for continuing declines in crime up to 2020 given the ~20-year lag, strengthening ⓐ.

h3.text: The sharp decline in violent crime in the US began in the 1990s rather than the 1970s.

h4.text: The decline in crime does not match the reduction of lead in gasoline that began in the 1970s.

b.note: The naive attack rb1 assumes an immediate effect, but the ~20-year time lag (c4) undercuts this inference.

h5.text: American adolescents who committed crimes had four times the bone lead content of those who did not.

h6.text: Higher individual lead exposure is positively correlated with criminal behavior in adolescents.

c.note: Direct empirical evidence linking criminal behavior with elevated lead levels provides an additional supporting argument for ⓐ.

A.summary: Survey the single polling station whose vote difference from the district total was smallest in the previous election.

B.summary: Stratify polling stations with similar party results from the previous election and randomly sample stations from each stratum.

C.summary: Travel to all polling stations in the district, surveying each station in proportion to its eligible voters.

c1.text: Method A surveys the station with the smallest past vote difference to represent the district.

c2.text: Method B stratifies polling stations by past party results and samples from each stratum.

c3.text: Method C visits all polling stations in sequence for a set time, sampling proportionally to eligible voters.

c4.text: Method A assumes that voting patterns at the selected polling station remain stable and consistent with the previous election.

c6.text: Method A is difficult to apply.

c7.text: Method B assumes that polling stations across the district are heterogeneous in voter political orientation.

c8.text: Method B assumes that polling stations within the same district are generally homogeneous in terms of voters' political orientation.

c9.text: Data from the previous election about vote counts per polling station is essential for Method C.

h1.text: There has been significant change in the population's social characteristics in a polling station since the last election.

h2.text: Past election results no longer reflect current voting patterns for that station.

a.note: Significant demographic changes undermine the assumption of historical stability (c4), concluding c6 and putting c5 OUT.

b.note: Method B stratifies because polling stations are heterogeneous (c7); it does not assume they are homogeneous (c8).

c.note: Method C visits all stations and only samples proportionally to current eligible voters, so prior election data is not assumed or needed.

Alice.summary: The Cool Summer Policy will reduce the stability of electricity supply by increasing summer peak demand.

Bob.summary: Switching to a flat rate system (1600 won base, 180 won/kWh) is better for lowering the summer bill burden for most households.

Charlie.summary: The Cool Summer Policy should be modified so that it applies only to vulnerable groups.

c1.text: To ensure stable supply, generation facilities must meet peak hourly electricity demand.

c2.text: The Cool Summer Policy expands tier limits in summer, effectively lowering electricity rates.

c3.text: Lowering electricity rates in summer increases summer peak hourly electricity demand.

c4.text: Summer peak hourly electricity demand is the critical peak determining generation capacity strain.

c5.text: The introduction of the Cool Summer Policy will reduce the stability of electricity supply.

c6.text: A flat rate system with 1,600 won base and 180 won/kWh lowers the summer bill burden for most households compared to the Cool Summer Policy.

c7.text: It is better to switch from the Cool Summer Policy to the flat rate system.

c8.text: The flat rate system results in a higher bill than the Cool Summer Policy for households consuming 400-450 kWh.

c9.text: Vulnerable groups benefit financially from the Cool Summer Policy.

c10.text: The Cool Summer Policy should apply only to vulnerable groups.

c11.text: Vulnerable groups using less than 200 kWh per month receive zero discount from the Cool Summer Policy.

h1.text: Peak hourly electricity consumption in Country X occurs in summer.

h2.text: Summer peak demand does not determine system capacity strain.

a.note: Summer peak being the actual highest peak supports rather than weakens Alice's premise (c4); the naive weakening rule ra1 fails.

h3.text: Most households consume 400–450 kWh per month.

b.note: At 400-450 kWh, Bob's flat rate yields a higher bill than the Cool Summer Policy, directly undermining Bob's premise c6.

h4.text: Most vulnerable individuals use less than 200 kWh per month.

c.note: Households under 200 kWh were already in Tier 1 and receive zero rate reduction, undermining Charlie's welfare premise c9.

Hypothesis 1.summary: People choose actions that maximize their expected payoff.

Hypothesis 2.summary: The more people believe their advantageous but unfair actions are unlikely to be detected, the more likely they are to engage in them.

c1.text: People choose actions that maximize their expected payoff.

c2.text: The more people believe their advantageous but unfair actions are unlikely to be detected by the other party, the more likely they are to engage in such actions.

h1.text: 60% of responders rejected the 8-2 offer in [Experiment 1].

h2.text: Responders chose 0 won over 2,000 won, failing to choose the action that maximizes expected payoff.

h3.text: People do not always choose actions that maximize their expected payoff.

a.note: Rejecting 2,000 won for 0 won contradicts expected payoff maximization, undermining Hypothesis 1.

h4.text: In [Experiment 1], a proposer believes acceptance probabilities for 5-5, 8-2, and Coin are 100%, 20%, and 80%, and chooses the Coin Option.

h5.text: Expected payoffs are 5,000 won for 5-5, 1,600 won for 8-2, and 5,200 won for Coin, making Coin the expected payoff-maximizing action.

b.note: The proposer selects the option with the highest expected payoff (5,200 won), which provides evidence confirming Hypothesis 1.

h6.text: Participants view 5-5 and Coin as fair and 8-2 as unfair, and the rate of proposers choosing 8-2 is higher in [Experiment 2] than in [Experiment 1].

h7.text: In Experiment 2, the proposer believes unfair actions can be obscured by the coin toss, increasing the rate of choosing unfair actions.

c.note: Proposers choose the unfair 8-2 option more when it can be disguised as a coin outcome, directly supporting Hypothesis 2.

CRS.summary: Understanding word meaning depends on understanding and following usage rules; failing to understand usage rules means failing to understand word meaning.

The following argument.summary: Conceptual role semantics leads to an infinite regress, so no one can understand the meaning of any word, refuting CRS.

c1.text: Understanding word meaning requires understanding the usage rules of that word.

c2.text: Following usage rules means using the word based on an understanding of those rules.

c3.text: Failing to understand the usage rules of a word means failing to understand the meaning of that word.

c4.text: To understand usage rules, those rules must first be expressed linguistically and clearly.

c5.text: Linguistic expressions of rules contain multiple words.

c6.text: To understand a rule, one must understand the meanings of all words included in its linguistic expression.

c7.text: An infinite regress occurs when understanding rule words requires understanding their rules, and so on.

c8.text: Infinite regress entails that no one can understand the meaning of any word.

c9.text: That no one understands the meaning of any word is absurd/unreasonable.

c10.text: Conceptual role semantics must be rejected.

h1.text: An artificial intelligence appears that can use Korean perfectly, as well as a native Korean.

1.note: Mere behavioral competence of AI without establishing whether it understands rules does not affect CRS, so CRS is not weakened.

h2.text: Rules for word usage do not necessarily have to be expressed linguistically.

2.note: Denying that rules must be linguistically expressed directly undermines premise c4 of the counterargument.

h3.text: A person in fact understands the meaning of every word included in the definition of 'ppyojukhada'.

3.note: CRS already assumes speakers understand meanings; showing a person understands words merely affirms empirical fact without providing a new argument or strengthening CRS.

h4.text: It is possible to understand the meaning of a statement even if it contains words whose meanings one does not understand.

4.note: Being able to understand a rule without understanding all constituent words directly undermines premise c6 of the counterargument.

h5.text: An agent does not understand the meaning of a word but can use it according to the usage rules.

5.note: CRS defines understanding meaning by understanding rules (not merely using per rules); an agent following rules without understanding meaning is not a counterexample.
